title: Will Bad Weather Disrupt Thanksgiving Travel?
author: Simmone Shah
body:
Millions are expected to travel this week ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday, but stormy weather and coastal flooding in parts of the country could disrupt plans during one of the year’s busiest travel periods. AAA projects 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles from home for Thanksgiving between Tuesday, Nov. 24 and Monday, Nov. 30.

On the East Coast, a developing nor’easter is expected to bring heavy rain, winds, and coastal flooding to the Southeast, impacting Florida and the Carolinas on Wednesday, before spreading upwards into the mid-Atlantic and Northeast on Thanksgiving Day.

The National Weather Service forecasts wind gusts of more than 40 mph inland along the I-95 corridor, a major highway that connects 15 states and Washington, D.C. Major airports could also see weather-related delays—just as airports are recovering from lingering disruptions caused by tech outages and a rare nationwide ground stop.

New York City is also expected to see heavy rain on Thanksgiving day. The city’s emergency management department warned residents and visitors to keep an eye out for “fowl weather” ahead of the holiday. “Keep an eye on Thursday,” it said on X. “The forecast shows a storm that could bring strong winds, rain, and coastal flooding to the city on Thanksgiving Day, with gusts of 40 to 45 mph possible and 1 to 2 inches of rain.”

It remains to be seen if the weather will impact the annual Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. According to city regulations, the parade’s balloons cannot fly if sustained winds exceed 23 mph or gusts exceed 34 mph.

With a full moon on Tuesday, the West Coast is also gearing up for the highest tides of the year, coupled with an incoming storm. A coastal flood advisory is in effect for the Pacific Northwest and parts of California.

The region has been battered by rain in the last few months, in large part due to a record-strong El Niño, and is still recovering from another powerful storm and high-tide flooding that hit earlier this month.

The worst rain is expected to come late Wednesday into Thursday, with another storm expected Friday evening. The combination of heavy rain and strong king tides could worsen the effects of other hazards—like flooding and coastal erosion.

San Francisco mayor Daniel Lurie urged residents to avoid traveling in the days ahead of the holiday.

“We know people are planning to visit family and friends but if you don’t need to, please don’t travel into the city,” he said. “We always want visitors, but these are special circumstances.”
